https://lowcinema.com/movie/night-owl-my.description: We'll be watching something that is Japanese with gross bugs that are a common problem in many homes.
Join us for another mystery VHS night presented by the folks at Night Owl Video.

https://lowcinema.com/movie/notes-on-bre.description: Dir. Bertram Könighofer & David Kleinl, 2006, Austria, German/English w/ subtitles, 31 min.

https://lowcinema.com/movie/screen-slate.description: Screen Slate’s Jon Dieringer, returning from a West Coast research and fact-finding mission, heads directly to Low Cinema to spiritually cleanse with a mystery 16mm screening. The 87-minute film was shot on location across Burbank, Malibu, and Pomona. Its director boasts that it predicted the invention of punk and school shootings. The print is in immaculate condition.

https://lowcinema.com/movie/singles/.description: Set in Seattle's grunge scene, Cameron Crowe's directorial sophomore feature is the '90s distilled into an essential oil. The fleamarket-furnished coffee shops serve up dark roast java while Gen Xers try — and fail — to resist the pressures of the corporate rat race. Cringe from beginning to end but with an aura of authenticity bequeathed by three decades of cultural amnesia, Singles is required viewing for anyone trying to understand the country's slow crawl from 1960s trust fund idealism to 2000s' tech monoculture.

https://lowcinema.com/movie/society/.description: A teenager in Beverly Hills begins to suspect that his wealthy parents are part of a gruesome cult made up of the social elite.

https://lowcinema.com/movie/stolen-kingd.description: The history of misdeeds and debauchery at Walt Disney World Resort over 30 years, which leads to the theft of almost half a million dollars worth of stolen props.

https://lowcinema.com/movie/surf-nazis-m.description: An earthquake leaves the California coastline in ruins and reduces the beaches to a state of chaos. A group of neo-Nazis takes advantage of the resulting chaos by fighting off several rival surfer gangs to seize control of the beaches.

https://lowcinema.com/movie/the-guyver/.description: When a researcher at the Chronos Corporation is mysteriously killed, his daughter (Vivian Wu) ; her boyfriend, Sean (Jack Armstrong) ; and a rogue CIA agent named Max Reed (Mark Hamill) all suspect foul play. Sean discovers a top-secret suit of Chronos armor called "the Guyver," which fuses to his body when he tries it on, turning him into a supremely powerful cyborg. Chronos' evil CEO, Fulton Balcus (David Gale), is enraged and sends a crew of mutant alien monsters to get the Guyver back.

https://lowcinema.com/movie/the-history-.description: A filmmaker applies lessons from a Hallmark movie writing workshop to pitch a documentary about concrete.

https://lowcinema.com/movie/twice-upon-a.description: In a land where dreams are born, the evil Synonamess Botch sets in motion a plan to give humanity non-stop nightmares that threatens the flow of time itself. Only a motley crew of creatures, including an adorable shapeshifter, a floral aspiring actress, a snarky Fairy Godmother, and a mime straight out of the silent film era, can save both the world and people's sleeping habits.

https://lowcinema.com/movie/wild-inside/.description: A Eurasian Eagle-Owl named Flaco escapes from the Central Park Zoo and sets off on a magical odyssey through the island of Manhattan. Flaco overcomes his years of captivity and lack of survival skills to answer the call of the wild – and discovers he was wild inside all along.

https://metrograph.com/film/9999000006-g.description: The Fu-Ho Grand, a movie palace in Taipei, is closing its doors. Its valedictory screening: King Hu’s 1967 wuxia epic Dragon Inn, playing to a motley smattering of spectators, including two stars of Hu’s original opus, Miao Tien and Shih Chun, watching their younger selves with tears in their eyes.

https://metrograph.com/film/9999000057-t.description: One breathtaking composition follows another in Scorsese’s adaptation of Edith Wharton’s Pulitzer Prize–winning masterpiece about social mores (and taboos) amongst New York’s viperous moneyed classes in late 19th-century New York, brought to life by an all-star lineup of craftspeople including cinematographer Michael Ballhaus, editor Thelma Schoonmaker, production designer Dante Ferretti, and composer Elmer Bernstein. In front of the camera there are Daniel Day-Lewis and Michelle Pfeiffer suffering beautifully as wealthy lawyer Newland Archer and Countess Ellen Olenska, the divorced pariah whom he yearns for, and Winona Ryder as Archer’s fiancée and, eventually, wife—outwardly a winsome innocent, but a cunning, cutthroat strategist where affairs of the heart are concerned. It was, Ryder stated during a recent appearance on (of all things) Hot Ones, “The role of a lifetime.” Part of Winona Ryder Analogue Youth

https://metrograph.com/film/9999000181-h.description: Kurosawa’s formal genius and rare humanism are on full display in this white-knuckle thriller—source of an upcoming remake by Spike Lee—which transposes the materials of an Ed McBain novel to contemporary Japan, starring Toshiro Mifune as a rich industrialist thrown into a nerve-shredding situation after, first believing his son has been kidnapped, discovering that his chauffeur’s child was taken by accident. Boasting nigh-constant visual invention, geometric precision of framing, an inventive narrative structure, and a bevy of staggering set pieces—the train hand-off! the down-and-dirty G.I. bar!—High & Low is a virtuoso work that’s also a deeply moral one, exploring the meaning of “justice” in a society defined by vast economic disparity. “High and Low has one of the most iconic train scenes of all time. And though it’s only one of many segments, the entire, wildly careening film has the feeling of a train in the slow-motion throes of derailment.” —Series curator Genevieve Yue Part of Trains: Local Routes

https://metrograph.com/film/9999000341-t.description: The cross-breeding of video games and cinema began in earnest with Tron, one of the first films to extensively employ CGI, here depicting the darkly glittering digital world inside a mainframe computer that programmer Jeff Bridges must compete in a series of gladiatorial contests in order to escape. Part of A Cyberpunk Canon

https://metrograph.com/film/9999000356-b.description: Ground into despairing dust by his routine as a low-level bureaucrat in an Orwellian near-future—drabulously conceived as a junk shop jumble by art directors Norman Garwood and Maggie Gray—Sam (Jonathan Pryce) takes flight only in his imagination, where he plays the winged savior to distressed damsel Kim Griest. A chance teleprinter error at work and a wrongful arrest, however, set Sam on a course for real adventure, one involving his dream girl’s truck-driving double, a suspected terrorist (Robert De Niro), a freakshow cocktail party, plastic surgery disasters, and much more outlandishness besides. “A melancholy, joke-ridden view of the horribleness of where we are now and the worst horribleness of where we’re heading… It’s like a stoned, slapstick 1984: a nightmare comedy in which the comedy is just an aspect of the nightmarishness.” —Pauline Kael, The New Yorker Part of The Office of Emptiness

https://metrograph.com/film/9999000422-f.description: Join Fireflies Press and Metrograph on Sunday, September 27 for the NYC launch of author and critic Anwen Crawford’s Morvern Callar. Her lyrical monograph on Lynne Ramsay’s film of the same name is the latest title in Fireflies Press’ 10-book Decadent Editions series, each spotlighting a milestone of contemporary cinema. Following the screening of Ramsay’s film, introduced by Fireflies Press co-publisher Annabel Brady-Brown, books will be available for purchase in the Lobby. A sensory odyssey packed into an intimate story of love, death, and theft, Lynne Ramsay’s second feature stays close to its impossibly distant title character, played with a transfixing inscrutability by Samantha Morton. Passing off the work of her suicided boyfriend as her own, Morvern gets a book deal and a ticket out of gray Scotland to sunny seaside Spain for herself and her best friend (Kathleen McDermott). A film of mysterious gestures, a hieroglyph that begs to be decoded while withholding the key. 35mm print courtesy of BFI National Archive Introduction by Fireflies Press co-publisher, Annabel Brady-Brown on Sunday, September 27th

https://metrograph.com/film/9999000425-n.description: Akerman was 26 years old and living in New York City, away from her native Belgium and her mother, when she teamed with DP Babette Mangolte to film this diary/essay/poem in subway stations and on street corners, their images to eventually be paired with Akerman’s recitals of her mother’s fretful letters. Arguably this extraordinary filmmaker’s most perfect and poignant nonfiction work, both one of the greatest portraits of a city ever put on film and a troubling, touching depiction of maternal love. Screens in the English-language version. “Though Chantal Akerman’s voice can be heard throughout News from Home, her image is only briefly glimpsed, in a reflection on the train. We can’t quite see her, but others undoubtedly can—men, especially, gawk unashamedly, a reminder that the graffiti-covered subway of 1976 New York was often a place of danger and hostility.” —Series curator Genevieve Yue Part of Trains: Local Routes

https://metrograph.com/film/9999000475-t.description: Before scaling Brokeback Mountain, Taiwanese American director Lee made this indie breakout about Wai Tung (Winston Chao, in his film debut), a gay man happily living in Manhattan with his partner who stages a sham marriage between himself and a penniless immigrant artist from mainland China in his building (May Chin) in order to please his traditionally minded parents—only to be appalled when they insist on throwing the “newlyweds” a whopper of a wedding party. A tender, emotionally grounded, sharply observed comedy of clashing cultures that’s made all the more poignant by its function as a time capsule of ’90s NYC. Part of Jiā: Histories of Home

https://metrograph.com/film/9999000490-o.description: Homer with a ball-peen hammer. Kidnapped and stuffed in a hole without explanation for 15 years of solitary confinement, when Oh Dae-su (Choi Min-sik) is suddenly let loose on the streets, he’s stone-cold pissed off and very, very dangerous. Winner of the Grand Prix at Cannes and an international pop phenomenon, Oldboy was a revenge thriller unlike any that had come before, featuring passages of pure bravura filmmaking (that one-shot hallway donnybrook!) and surreal sicko humor that’ll put you off of sushi for a while. “Put together with brutally uncompromising style [and] the cold-steel edge of a knife against your throat. A dark and thrillingly horrible adventure into the realms of the unthinkable.” —The Guardian Part of Classical Cinema

https://metrograph.com/film/9999000497-h.description: Hong Kong cinema superstars Tony Leung and Leslie Cheung play a pair of lovers living out the waning days of their relationship as expatriates in Buenos Aires. Lusty tango bars, the salsa music of the La Boca sidewalks, and a hypnotic visit to the nearby Iguazu Falls give further dimension to the tensions growing between the two. Winner of the Best Director prize at the 1997 Cannes Film Festival, Wong’s Happy Together is a stunning display of filmmaking style and a touching story of love on the brink of dissolution. Part of Like the Wind: Lensed by Christopher Doyle

https://metrograph.com/film/9999000610-a.description: Perhaps the very finest of Sirk’s Ross Hunter-produced melodramas, All That Heaven Allows pairs Jane Wyman and Rock Hudson as, respectively, a well-off widow in country club Connecticut, and the broad-necked, Thoreau-reading gardener who she falls for. Her priggish children, aghast, conspire to break off the pairing, an endeavor that ends in a bone-chilling Christmas conciliation—the presentation of a gift television set as a kind of death sentence. Of this scene Rainer Werner Fassbinder, profoundly marked by his encounter with Sirk’s film, would write: “At that point everyone in the moviehouse breaks down. They suddenly understand something about the world and what it does to people.” Right on. Part of The Leaves Are Falling

https://metrograph.com/film/9999000668-s.description: “Criss cross.” Hitchcock’s adaptation of Highsmith’s 1951 page-turner kicks off with a casual encounter that reads like a same-sex pickup, as tennis star Guy Haines (Farley Granger) inadvertently agrees to “swap murders” with preening rich kid Bruno Anthony (Robert Walker, in a career performance), and continues through some of the finest set pieces of Hitch’s career: a tennis match at Forest Hills, Bruno stalking his prey through a vulgar county fair, and an out-of-control carousel. “In Hitchcock, the people you meet on trains can spell romance, adventure, or, in the case of Strangers on a Train’s Guy Haines, a colossal headache! Tip: beware anyone wearing spectator shoes.” —Series curator Genevieve Yue Part of Trains: Local Routes

https://metrograph.com/film/9999000710-g.description: “My codename is Project 2501, and I am a life form that was born in a sea of information.” In the year 2029, the world looks like a hybridization of Hong Kong, Tokyo, and New York, yielding to entropy and technocracy. Cyborg Major Kusanagi, a perfect specimen of human-brained computer engineering is on the case to track and destroy an omnipotent entity known as The Puppet Master—a hacker? a virus?—who threatens world order. Her physical and existential journey deftly detailed by Oshii’s animation, combining traditional hand-drawn cells and computer-generated graphics, creating a haunting, awe-inspiring magnum opus. Part of A Cyberpunk Canon

https://metrograph.com/film/9999000718-b.description: While so many special effects spectacles are lost in time like tears in the rain, Blade Runner remains the template for imagining the neon-wreathed downer of the future, every bit as influential in its vision as was Fritz Lang’s Metropolis over a half century before. Working from a novel by cult writer Philip K. Dick to create a film that would become the gold standard for sci-fi noir, director Scott shares credit here with “visual futurist” Syd Mead’s design concepts and synth pioneer Vangelis’s atmospheric score. Part of A Cyberpunk Canon

https://metrograph.com/film/9999000719-t.description: Too many sequels and an incalculable cultural impact later, it’s sometimes forgotten what a hot and nasty little movie Cameron’s original Terminator was, dropping peak-physique Schwarzenegger into a sleazy Los Angeles of leather bars, punk rockers, and skid rows, where he quickly proceeds to killing cops by the score and tracking down mother-to-be of humankind’s savior Linda Hamilton. Working for the very last time with budget constraints, Cameron—and FX gurus Stan Winston and Gene Warren Jr.—deliver the goods and how, in a grimy lil’ chef d’oeuvre that gave us Cyberdine, Skynet, and a whole lexicon for discussing extinction-level singularity events. Part of A Cyberpunk Canon

https://metrograph.com/film/9999000720-r.description: I’d buy that for a dollar! For a strange few years, beginning with this runaway hit, the perverse imagination and earthy humor of Verhoeven seemed to sync up perfectly with the desires of the American multiplex-going public. In dystopian Detroit, private sector Omni Consumer Products have taken over policing and made the ultimate law enforcement machine from leftover pieces of peace officer Peter Weller—but they didn’t bank on their invention making his way up the corporate ladder of crime. A frightfully funny vision of a post-industrial cybernetic future, with Kurtwood Smith, Ronny Cox, and Muguel Ferrer an impressive trifecta of irredeemable scumbags. Part of A Cyberpunk Canon

https://metrograph.com/film/9999000735-c.description: A hot-shot to the heart, pop masterpiece Chungking Express tells the stories of two lovelorn cops (Takeshi Kaneshiro and Tony Leung) and the women who baffle them (Brigitte Lin and Faye Wong, who contributes a Cantopop cover of The Cranberries’ “Dreams”), its bifurcated structure suggesting the A- and B-sides of a 45. Wong’s international breakthrough introduced new audiences to his rich, sensorial brand of filmmaking, inviting one to disappear into, sink into, live inside, a voluptuary world bigger and brighter than our own—but just as heartbreaking. Part of Like the Wind: Lensed by Christopher Doyle

https://metrograph.com/film/9999000795-t.description: Marion Cotillard has one of her greatest roles as Ewa, a Polish Catholic immigrant newly arrived in Ellis Island, trying to find the means to free her sister from quarantine in a c. 1921 New York City that’s full of lures and snares, among them Joaquin Phoenix’s smalltime pimp and tinhorn impresario and Jeremy Renner’s Bowery illusionist. A richly textured film of disarming depths of feeling from Gray, whose beguiling closing shot resonates long after the credits roll. “We effectively destroyed the film negative with various techniques,” said Darius Khondji, “to achieve the desired emotional aesthetic of that era.” Part of Radical Chiaroscuro: The Work of Darius Khondji

https://metrograph.com/film/9999000844-a.description: Ozu’s gorgeous 53rd and final feature is a return to a favorite theme, the poignant comedy of marriage, with beloved regular Chishu Ryu as a father giving away his daughter and preparing for another, final goodbye. Good Morning’s satire of creeping consumerism has become more bitter here, the feeling of incoming winter chill is sharper, the entire project imbued with a tang of regret—incidentally, the title literally translates to “The Taste of Autumn Mackerel.” Part of The Leaves Are Falling

https://metrograph.com/film/9999000918-t.description: Lower East Side native Walter Matthau wears perhaps the broadest tie in film history as a grousing Transit Authority lieutenant who gets an unlikely shot at heroism when a group of criminals take a downtown 6 train hostage and demand a million dollars from the flat-broke city. Engineered with perfect pace and verve by the underrated Sargent, with growly, jowly Matthau at his hangdog best. “Featuring one of the grittiest New Yorkers ever seen on film: the ruddy-cheeked wino who, despite the commotion on her hijacked 6 train, sleeps through the entire ordeal.” —Series curator Genevieve Yue Introduction by Genevieve Yue and Erika Balsom, with a book signing following the screening, on Saturday, October 3rd Part of Trains: Local Routes

https://metrograph.com/film/9999000929-t.description: That the world of the future was to be increasingly shaped by Asia was a central tenet of cyberpunk, and so it should come as no surprise that one of the greatest of cyberpunk films came from the Land of the Rising Sun. Man and machine feel the urge to merge in Tsukamoto’s utterly indescribable midnight movie staple, an assault-on-the-senses body horror running of the gauntlet which centers on an anonymous salaryman who begins to transform himself into a man of steel, his waking nightmare captured in twitchy camerawork and lurid, gritty black-and-white 16mm. A symphony of sex, steel, and scarification, set to a scraping industrial clangor. Part of A Cyberpunk Canon

https://metrograph.com/film/9999001169-a.description: “All the President’s Men had to be on my list because it inspired me and so many other journalists to serve as watchdog press, and because so many recent events are reminiscent of Nixon and Watergate.” —Kimberley Reed Robert Redford and Dustin Hoffman star as newsmen Carl Bernstein and Bob Woodward in Pakula’s riveting retelling of the startling series of true events whereby the assignment of two Washington Post reporters to investigate the suspiciously urgent Republican response to what appears to be just an amateurish break-in at the Democratic Party National headquarters at the Watergate Hotel would lead to the toppling of a president. The process of investigative journalism rendered as high drama, its unerring eye for realistic detail extending to a scrupulous reproduction of the Post’s newsroom floor." Q&A with Carl Bernstein and Maggie Haberman, White House correspondent for The New York Times, moderated by Natalie Kitroeff of “The Daily” on Sunday, October 18th Part of The New York Times presents Stop the Presses

https://metrograph.com/film/9999001188-r.description: “He has his father’s eyes…” Satanists are on the loose in Central Park West in Polanski’s slow-burn thriller, which slips almost imperceptibly from the quotidian into the profane, and gives new meaning to the phrase “pregnancy scare.” Young marrieds Mia Farrow and John Cassavetes make friendly with their elder neighbors Ruth Gordon and Sidney Blackmer, but when Farrow’s abandoned and isolated Rosemary goes into a paranoiac tailspin while expecting her first child, she begins to wonder why everyone is so very eager for her to take her daily dosage of tannis root… A masterclass in slow-building, spine-tingling suspense, aided immeasurably by the dab-handed work of legendary editor Sam O’Steen. Part of Filmcraft: American Cinema Editors

https://metrograph.com/film/9999001199-b.description: Coppola at his most boldly baroque, Gary Oldman wearing cinema’s most iconic updo, a puppyish young Keanu Reeves trying to make his way back to Winona Ryder, and Anthony Hopkins as vampire hunter Abraham Van Helsing—it’s all here in this opulent production which returns to the original Stoker text and draws out the piercing sexual ache and romantic longing implicit therein. Part of Winona Ryder Analogue Youth

https://metrograph.com/film/9999001293-y.description: The last work of a master filmmaker who died far too young, the gentle, restrained, and terribly humane Yi Yi observes the interplay between three generations of an upper middle-class Taipei family. Comic when dealing in the foibles of its excellent ensemble cast and the mores of the urban bourgeoise, yet also possessed throughout by an air of unmistakable melancholy and lingering regret at missed opportunities, this feeling made all the deeper when one considers the great films Yang might still have produced. A work of epic length that avoids even a hint of bombast, dedicated instead to working its way into the hidden, niche spaces of everyday people’s emotional lives, it’s a film as rich and as sad as life itself. Part of Jiā: Histories of Home

https://metrograph.com/film/9999001343-t.description: This sprightly interpretation of Hans Christian Anderson’s story was eyed by Disney as far back as the days of Snow White and the Seven Dwarves, finally surfacing in 1989. There’s a hot crustacean band, sure, but also a keening grasp of the angst, loneliness, and longing in Anderson’s tale, encapsulated in Ariel’s dream of being “Part of Your World,” a highlight of Alan Mencken and Howard Ashman's superlative songbook. Part of It Started With A Mouse: Hand-Drawn Classics on 35

https://metrograph.com/film/9999001463-m.description: It’s 1963, and different-drummer single mother Cher has decided to move from Oklahoma to smalltown Massachusetts, uprooting her two daughters, nine-year-old Kate and Catholicism-obsessed 15-year-old Rachel (Winona Ryder, who provides the narration). What follows includes JFK assassination trauma, a pregnancy scare, mother-daughter sexual competition, and one miraculous rescue, with devastating dynamic duo Cher and Ryder pushing one another to histrionic heights. Part of Winona Ryder Analogue Youth

https://metrograph.com/film/9999001550-s.description: From first kisses to more sinister secrets, all of the loneliness and wonderment and danger and astonishing endurance that distinguish the years we pass between infancy and adolescence are contained here in Truffaut’s string of loosely connected vignettes concerning a group of schoolchildren living in the provincial town of Thiers in central France and their very involved instructor (Jean-François Stévenin). A film brimming with pleasures for children and adults both, unmistakably sweet-spirited while refreshingly free of sentimental treacle. “A comedy, a romance, a mystery—in a word: childhood—captured, distilled, and transformed effortlessly from sketchbook to symphony in the hands of a master.” —Wes Anderson Part of Screen Time at Metrograph

https://metrograph.com/film/9999001554-t.description: A surreal nocturnal animated odyssey from Yuasa, the mad genius behind Mind Game, rendered in a frenetic, galaxy-brained, endlessly morphing style. The Night is Short, Walk on Girl follows a mysterious high schooler known only as The Girl with Black Hair through the streets of Kyoto’s famed Ponto-Cho party district, drinking middle-aged salarymen under the table when she’s not mixing with barflies, obsessive collectors, and guerilla theater performers, all the while oblivious to the efforts of a fellow student who has been creating increasingly fantastic and contrived reasons to run into her in a gambit to win her love. A comic fable of fleeting youthful passions, as lived out through one mad, unforgettable night. Part of This Night Has Opened My Eyes

https://metrograph.com/film/9999001577-t.description: A big-screen outing for this flight of feline fun from the Disney vaults, the last animated feature to be signed off on by Walt himself is a purr-fect Parisian period piece featuring a family of nose-in-the-air cats who, after being kidnapped away from the accustomed baronial splendor of their home, have to rely on the streetwise wiles of alley cat O’Malley to keep them safe. Featuring animation supremely attentive to the syntax of kitty motion and the vocal talents of Eva Gabor and Scatman Crothers who gets to lead on the boppin' classic “Everybody Wants to Be a Cat.” Part of It Started With A Mouse: Hand-Drawn Classics on 35

https://metrograph.com/film/9999001726-t.description: A phantasmagoric, definition-defying film from perhaps France’s premier underground filmmaker, The Treasure of Bitch Islands begins with the mysterious disappearance of an engineer who has discovered a new energy source, and follows a post-nuclear Ulysses’s voyage to locate the substances used in the engineer’s formula, only to be found and harvested on an island of mad scientists and headhunters. An anarchic allegory with a punky sensibility, part Guy Maddin pastiche, part surrealist mix-and-match, and pure cult classic. “The shoot was madness, and some of us risked our lives a few times, especially while doing a scene on the edge of this huge volcano. Ossang was really more like a rock star than a film director… I shot the film completely inspired by him and his energy, even if I was sometimes terrified.” —Darius Khondji Part of Radical Chiaroscuro: The Work of Darius Khondji

https://metrograph.com/film/9999001729-a.description: The fourth entry in the Alien series brings Sigourney Weaver’s Lt. Ellen Ripley, last seen swan diving into a vat of molten steel, back from the Great Beyond—after a fashion, at least. Cloned from samples of extraterrestrial-contaminated DNA, Ripley 2.0 finds herself aboard the USM Auriga spaceship two centuries after her original’s death, and shortly thereafter contending with a new host of Xenomorphs, both fangsome foes and, now, blood relations. “Jean-Pierre… wanted to make a film that was closer to his universe, with plenty of dark humor in it… The hallways were purposely lit with green hues, which would make the actors’ skin tones come out colder… With the help of the production designer, Nigel Phelps, and the vision of Jean-Pierre, we managed in the end to make a very different kind of Alien movie.” —Darius Khondji Part of Radical Chiaroscuro: The Work of Darius Khondji

https://metrograph.com/film/9999001730-e.description: Don’t cry for her, Argentina—after years of dauntless campaigning, Madonna landed the coveted role of actress-cum-First Lady Eva Perón in this lavish, costume-change-a-minute adaptation of Tim Rice and Andrew Lloyd Webber’s 1978 stage musical, featuring Jonathan Pryce as the statesman who shares his power and his bed with Eva, and Antonio Banderas as narrator of her meteoric rise and tragic end. “Evita is actually a very visual movie, and Alan Parker is probably one of the most exciting and visual directors I have ever worked with… He wanted to make the film look very real, almost like a newsreel, but also very glamorous at the same time… There were certain scenes where we had up to 4,000 or 5,000 extras, because Alan didn’t want to use any special effects—he wanted it all to be in front of the lens.” —Darius Khondji Part of Radical Chiaroscuro: The Work of Darius Khondji

https://metrograph.com/film/9999001733-t.description: A sort of Lord of the Flies for the jet-setting, designer drug-popping leisure class, Boyle’s adaptation of Alex Garland’s novel is a steamy thriller set in motion when Leonardo DiCaprio’s backpacking beach bum accepts an invitation to a pristine island in the Gulf of Thailand, his arrival in the fragile social ecosystem of permanent vacationers and marijuana farmers initiating a series of events that stir up trouble in paradise. “The Beach is a very sharp movie, and I always felt the story was like a blade that cuts and causes you to bleed: there’s blood on the sand and sharks in the water, and the people themselves behave like sharks. All this comes together to give you the look of a clear blue sky over a sandy beach that’s stained red. It’s a hyper-realistic image.” —Darius Khondji Part of Radical Chiaroscuro: The Work of Darius Khondji

https://metrograph.com/film/9999001734-a.description: For their study of an elderly couple—played by icons of French cinema Jean-Louis Trintignant and Emmanuelle Riva, both superlative—facing final separation by cruel death, Haneke and cinematographer Darius Khondji created a litany of framings that feel brittle in their composed beauty, each marked by an elegant exactitude and slowly suffocating airlessness. Hard and tender, this may be Haneke’s ultimate accomplishment—and, incidentally, a eulogy for the youthful dreams of the 1960s European art cinema. Part of Radical Chiaroscuro: The Work of Darius Khondji

https://metrograph.com/film/9999001736-o.description: The titular beast is a gentle, lumbering, lovable “super pig” created by big agribusiness, peacefully raised in the South Korean countryside by young Mija (Ahn Seo-hyun) before being spirited off to the US, sweeping both pet and owner into a conflict between animal rights activists and mercenary corporate forces. A dark science fiction fable, its impressive ensemble cast includes Tilda Swinton, Paul Dano, and Jake Gyllenhaal. “[Okja] represents a departure toward a different type of image, a different texture and look: something very blue and metallic, with lots of compressed cityscapes and a bit of gold in the flesh tones… [Visual effects supervisor Erik de Boer] sat in with us [during the color grading] where we took every single shot of Okja in the film and treated each one individually for aspects of color and light.” —Darius Khondji Part of Radical Chiaroscuro: The Work of Darius Khondji

https://metrograph.com/film/9999001984-n.description: Jarmusch’s career-long fascination with at-home-in-the-world wanderers finds its perfect expression in this anthology piece with a Tom Waits soundtrack and Independent Spirit Award-winning cinematography by Elmes, set simultaneously in five different cabs in five different cities around the world. In Los Angeles casting agent Gena Rowlands cross-examines driver Winona Ryder, Isaach De Bankolé drives a mysterious young blind woman through Paris, and the backseat operates everywhere as an analyst’s sofa, loneliness and urban anomie proving to know no national bounds. “Mr. Jarmusch again demonstrates his mastery of comedy of the oblique.”—The New York Times Part of Winona Ryder Analogue Youth

https://metrograph.com/film/9999002029-p.description: The fourth and final film by Kon takes place in a not-too-distant future in which therapists, using a new technology called DC Mini, are able to record the dreams of psychiatric patients. All well and good, until a raid on the lab leads to the loss of the DC Mini prototype and a bleed between the troubled subconscious images and reality, leading to a race-against-time to stop bedlam from breaking out in the streets. An admitted inspiration for Christopher Nolan’s Inception (2010), though far more visually extravagant in its vibrant, psychedelia-inflected imaginings, which climax in a thrilling, terrifying dream apocalypse burst from Kon’s fervid imagination. Part of A Cyberpunk Canon

https://metrograph.com/film/9999002034-m.description: Returning to the well of Greek myth, Pasolini fixed on the figure of Medea, the pagan priestess loved and left behind by the questing Jason, whose story became for Pasolini a symbol of the colonization of the classical world and the vanquishing of the precious forces of the irrational. Opera star Maria Callas, not singing and barely speaking in her only dramatic role, is riveting in her interpretation of the Medea of Euripides’s tragedy, a woman manipulated by a power-hungry adventurer, driven to vengeance by deceit. Part of Classical Cinema

https://metrograph.com/film/9999002042-o.description: Seeking source materials from which to forge a new “primal cinema,” Pasolini delved into the storehouse of mythic heritage. Taking on Sophocles’s Oedipus Rex, he begins with a prologue set in prewar Italy, and goes on to defy expectation throughout, depicting Oedipus (Franco Citti), unknowingly betrothed to biological mother Silvana Mangano, as a victim of his own ignorant innocence, here far from an unambiguously positive virtue. Pasolini’s first film in color, featuring costumes and art direction that evoke an almost science fiction vision of the ancient world, and a showy role for Carmelo Bene, then-reigning bad boy of Italian stage and screen. Part of Classical Cinema

https://metrograph.com/film/9999002231-l.description: Winona Ryder would receive an Academy Award nomination for Best Actress for her role as the headstrong, literary minded Jo March in Armstrong’s perfectly enchanting adaptation of Louisa May Alcott’s 1868 novel of the same name, about the travails of the March sisters of Concord, Massachusetts, and their various suitors. Made with sweet-spirited good humor and exacting attention to period detail, with Trini Alvarado, Samantha Mathis, Kirsten Dunst, and Claire Danes rounding out the March clan, and Eric Stoltz, Gabriel Byrne, and Christian Bale among the men drawn to the glow exuded by the March homestead. “Solid, warming, bountiful, brimful of high spirits, a glowing treat that belongs at the top of any holiday movie shopping list.” —Boston Globe

https://metrograph.com/film/9999002242-b.description: Lean’s simple, tender, and terribly emotionally direct film, featuring never-better Noël Coward dialogue and a Rachmaninoff theme that grows insuperably sad with repetition, follows an affair between a middle-class couple (Celia Johnson and Trevor Howard) who happen to be inconveniently married to other people, their mutual love and mutual agony increasing over the course of seven meetings and departures that begin with a chance in a railway station buffet. One of the great screen romances, full stop. “The trains are mercilessly exact in Brief Encounter—there’s only three minutes between the departures of the trains that take Laura and Alec away from each other, and they’re never late.” —Series curator Genevieve Yue 35mm print provided courtesy of the American Genre Film Archive. Introduction by Genevieve Yue on Saturday, September 5th Part of Trains: Local Routes

https://metrograph.com/film/9999002246-a.description: Part of Jiā: Histories of Home

https://metrograph.com/film/9999002255-u.description: Adam Sandler gives a career-best performance as Howard Ratner, a fast-talking jeweler in Manhattan’s Diamond District with a penchant for living on the edge and well beyond his means, in the Safdies’ hectic, often hilarious thriller, where a debt-saddled Howie makes a series of high-stakes parlay bets on Kevin Garnett’s performance in the 2012 NBA playoffs that could lead to the windfall of a lifetime—or the abrupt end of his gambling career. “It’s gritty, but in the ’80s sense of it—gritty, with a lot of light and contrast. I started being a cinematographer in the ’80s, so they went back to this period of time where we were after very strong, ink blacks, very long lenses, very contrast-y images, very harsh contours… It was completely unlike anything I’ve done. I would never have thought I would photograph one day a movie like this. But it ended up being my favorite work, probably.” —Darius Khondji Part of Radical Chiaroscuro: The Work of Darius Khondji

https://metrograph.com/film/9999002564-e.description: Jancsó’s radically original, downright hypnotic retelling of the Ancient Greek myth against the backdrop of the puszta, Hungary’s vast, muddy plains, is among the long-take master’s most bravura stylistic performances, its 70-minute runtime made up of only twelve intricately composed shots. Reworking the tale of Electra and her ill use at the hands of Aegisthus—the man who loved her mother and murdered her father 15 years ago—Jancsó produces a timeless meditation on tyranny and rebellion—and a resounding call to resistance. Part of Classical Cinema

https://metrograph.com/film/9999002965-s.description: Enthralling, haunting, hypnotic, enigmatic, visually stunning, and overwhelmingly emotional, Tarkovsky’s slow sci-fi epic—based on Polish author Stanisław Lem’s 1961 novel of the same name—follows psychologist Kris Kelvin (Donatas Banionis) on a voyage to a space station that’s orbiting the planet Solaris, where he’s been sent to investigate curious hallucinations amongst members of the research team manning it, only, upon arriving, to encounter his late wife, dead ten years, waiting for him… or at least something that looks and acts exactly like her. A singular odyssey into outer and inner space, posing questions about the nature of love and humanity that linger long after its celebrated final shot. Part of New Museum Presents New Humans

https://metrograph.com/film/9999002970-t.description: “Waaarriors! Come out and play-ay!” Falsely accused of responsibility for the assassination of New York’s most powerful ganglord during a citywide summit in the Bronx’s Van Cortlandt Park, Swan (Michael Beck) and his fellow Warriors now have to fight their way back, block by block and mano a mano, to the safe shores of their Coney Island turf. The film’s knuckle-busting action choreography and its vision of NYC as a coliseum-like proving grounds for epic heroism—its source, at a distance, is Xenophon’s 4th century BC Anabasis—are delectable, but its greatness lies in its attention to character, how it lets us see a crew of provincial Brooklynites gradually discovering they’re the toughest dudes in town. Part of Classical Cinema

https://metrograph.com/film/9999003028-r.description: Tsai’s first theatrically released film isn’t as pared down in its approach as some of his later works—it even has a rather catchy synth theme song!—but in most respects it’s pure Tsai, a film about urban loners and the city’s (largely unfulfilled) promises of connection and sexual intimacy. Lee Kang-sheng, Tsai’s acteur fétiche, stars as a teenaged Taipei arcade rat who develops an obsession with a young petty hoodlum (Chen Chao-jung) that’s a tangle of vengeful wrath and repressed lust. An extraordinary debut, in which aspects of all its maker’s films to come are visible. Part of Jiā: Histories of Home

https://metrograph.com/film/9999003057-d.description: A pivotal but little-screened film in Hou’s celebrated filmography, Daughter of the Nile acts as a sort of bridge between his breakthrough Coming of Age Trilogy and the trilogy of period-set films he made in collaboration with writer Wu Nien-jen. In this film, for the first time, Hou places contemporary Taipei center stage, telling the story of a young woman (pop star Lin Yang) trying to prevent her family from falling apart in a fast-changing city that offers its residents no sense of permanence or security. While Hou would explore Taipei’s complicated history in his films with Wu, in Daughter of the Nile he acutely diagnosed its present state. Part of Jiā: Histories of Home

https://metrograph.com/film/9999003126-w.description: Capping an incredible eight-year creative partnership with Almodóvar, repeat collaborator Carmen Maura here plays voice actress Pepa, who, abandoned by her lover, has resolved to kill herself by downing a batch of gazpacho laced with sleeping pills. That’s just the start of the orgy of unhinged behavior that makes up Almodóvar’s gaudy, cheeky screwball melodrama about Shiite terrorist cells and romance on the rocks, a camp romp celebration of emotional excess that has all the makings of an obscure cult classic, yet improbably became the highest-grossing Spanish film of all time upon release, and did its part in putting co-star Antonio Banderas on the international stage. Part of Among Friends

https://metrograph.com/film/9999003243-r.description: A precious glimpse into the creative process of the late synth-pop star, film composer, and activist Ryuichi Sakamoto, Schible’s deeply affecting film picks up with its introspective subject as he returns to music-making after having been diagnosed with cancer, channeling his new awareness of his mortality into his latest work. Part of Sakamoto on Screen Portraits of an Artist

https://metrograph.com/film/9999003314-s.description: After the death of her poet mother, 19-year-old American Lucy (Liv Tyler) travels to a Tuscan villa near Siena owned by family friends in hopes of exploring her family’s history and reuniting with her first kiss, though soon finds herself contending with a crowded field of would-be suitors. Working in his native Italy for the first time in 15 years, and in his only collaboration with DP Darius Khondji, Bertolucci creates a film of warm, mellow light; lyrical grace notes; and exquisite performances from Tyler, Joseph Fiennes, Jeremy Irons, Rachel Weisz, and others. Part of Radical Chiaroscuro: The Work of Darius Khondji

https://metrograph.com/film/9999003325-f.description: Part hard-boiled crime thriller and part soft, featherweight giddiness, Fallen Angels was first conceived as a segment of Wong’s Chungking Express, then developed into a darker companion piece to his glistening pop-romantic masterpiece, the story of a hitman (Leon Lai) looking to hang up his gun, the business partner (Michelle Reis) who quietly lusts after him, and a mute troublemaker (Takeshi Kaneshiro) running amok in Hong Kong. Christopher Doyle’s cinematography has never been more woozily, blearily beautiful, nor has the Fragrant Harbor ever been put on screen with such transfixing nocturnal glamor. Part of The Last Dreamers

https://metrograph.com/film/9999003369-h.description: “Dear Diary: My teen-angst bullshit now has a body count.” A caustic rejoinder to John Hughes’s ’80s Brat Pack pictures, Lehmann’s savage suburban satire brought out the sociopathic side of Christian Slater’s too-cool outlaw persona, casting him as J.D., the motorcycle-riding new arrival at Ohio’s Westerburg High School who recruits Winona Ryder’s at-first pliable Veronica Chandler into his increasingly unhinged plans to humble their class’s ruling clique of three terrible popular girls named Heather. Clearly having a ball with Daniel Waters’s imminently quotable, coal-black screenplay, Ryder gives more than a few line-readings for the ages here; just try to keep “What’s your damage?” out of your vocabulary after viewing. Part of Winona Ryder Analogue Youth

https://metrograph.com/film/9999003486-b.description: Imagined by writer-director Brooks as a romantic comedy with a “new kind of heroine,” his follow-up to the wildly successful Terms of Endearment focuses on a love triangle between brilliant, career-driven television news producer Jane Craig (Holly Hunter); her conscientious but camera-shy colleague, Aaron (Albert Brooks); and telegenic station newcomer Tom (William Hurt), the two men competing for an anchor job and the attentions of the disarmingly intense Jane. “In his first film since his Oscar-winning Terms of Endearment, Mr. Brooks goes inside the offices and studios of the Washington bureau of a national television network to show us how things work. As exposes go, Broadcast News is gentle. It's far more amused than angry. Its wit is decently humane.” —Vincent Canby, The New York Times Introduction by Michael Barbaro of "The Daily" on Saturday, October 17th Part of The New York Times presents Stop the Presses

https://metrograph.com/film/9999003500-p.description: Drawing on newly discovered home movies and a rich bounty of archival materials, Schiller’s trailblazing documentary, now marking its 30th anniversary, offers up a vibrant and vivacious evocation of the community of female artists and culturati of all stripes—among their number Gertrude Stein, Alice B. Toklas, Djuna Barnes, and Colette—who called Paris’s Left Bank home in the first decades of the previous century. A film that acts on the viewer like a tonic draught of fresh air, Paris Was a Woman is an enthralling evocation of one of the most storied periods in the history of the City of Light and of an anything-goes bohemian enclave that fostered both personal and creative liberation. New 4k Restoration created by IndieCollect in association with Women’s Film Preservation Fund A Zeitgeist Films release Q&A with filmmakers Greta Schiller and Andrea Weiss moderated by broadcast journalist Laura Flanders on Friday, October 16th Q&A with filmmakers Greta Schiller and Andrea Weiss moderated by Jane Gaines, Founder of Columbia University’s Women Film Pioneers Project, on Saturday, October 17th Introduction by Sandra Schulberg, President of IndieCollect, on Sunday, October 18th Book signing of Paris Was A Woman with author Andrea Weiss following all three screenings

https://metrograph.com/film/9999003555-t.description: Mann’s white-knuckle drama of white-collar whistleblowing and callous boardroom skullduggery stars Russell Crowe as tobacco industry research scientist Dr. Jeffrey Wigand and his Heat star Al Pacino as the 60 Minutes producer desperate to get the good doctor to spill his secrets on air, leading to a clash of corporate titans between Brown & Williamson tobacco and CBS News. Media manipulation, profits over people, and businesses operating like rogue states—Mann didn’t invent the 21st century, but he sure saw it coming. “Once Hollywood had a favorite folk tale: that the lone truth teller battling political or corporate evil would triumph, however bitterly, when the facts became known. But in the chillingly contemporary world of The Insider it's not that simple. Almost every character in the story is compromised by business considerations. And in the film's vision of television news reporting, moral relativism is a big part of playing the game.” —Janet Maslin, The New York Times Q&A to follow with investigative journalist Lowell Bergman, portrayed by Al Pacino in the film, and Pulitzer Prize-winning reporter and podcast host Pablo Torre on Saturday, October 17th Part of The New York Times presents Stop the Presses

https://metrograph.com/film/9999003587-t.description: Back in Hong Kong after taking his shot at conquering Hollywood, Tsui returned home with both barrels blazing, producing this high-strung action melodrama about a cash-strapped expectant father (Nicholas Tse) who joins the bodyguard service of his uncle (Anthong Wong) in order to make ends meet, only to discover—along with co-worker Wu Bai—a criminal conspiracy with international implications. Triad machinations, attempted assassinations, and top-tier stunt work courtesy choreographer Hung Yan-yan make Time and Tide essential viewing for any enthusiast of go-for-broke Hong Kong action. Part of Don't Play with Fire: The Films of Tsui Hark

https://metrograph.com/film/9999003673-l.description: A cinematic Molotov cocktail that was the first onscreen description of life (and death) in Paris’s banlieue housing projects that many French filmgoers had ever seen, La Haine depicts three armed and angry slum kids—Vincent Cassel, Hubert Koundé, and Saïd Taghmaoui—who, following days of rioting after the police’s savage beating of a young man, hit the city streets like ticking time bombs. A breakneck Steadicam journey through the concrete jungles of the suburbs, given an almost lunar desolation by the film’s black-and-white photography, La Haine is a propulsive, volatile, and visceral landmark of ’90s French cinema. Part of This Night Has Opened My Eyes

https://metrograph.com/film/9999003685-g.description: Based on a 1993 memoir of the same name by Susanna Kaysen, Mangold’s powerhouse picture sets its scene at a New England psychiatric hospital c. 1967 where Winona Ryder (in the Kaysen role; also a producer on the film) lands after suffering a nervous breakdown. Among the committed at Claymoore are a hall-of-fame lineup of ’90s female acting talent, including self-harmer Brittany Murphy, schizophrenic burn victim Elisabeth Moss and, in a star-making turn, Angelina Jolie as sociopath agitator Lisa Rowe. Ryder’s is not the flashiest role here, but she holds the film together with her quiet, alert intensity, offering a springboard for her co-stars to dive off into the deep end. Part of Winona Ryder Analogue Youth

https://metrograph.com/film/9999003694-t.description: Among the most perfectly cast Hollywood studio films of the last half-century, cinematographer-cum-director Sonnenfeld’s adaptation of Charles Addams’s macabre recurring New Yorker feature stars Raul Julia as the suave patriarch of the Addams clan (“You lady-killer…” “Acquitted!”), Anjelica Huston as his waxen, witchy bride, and an outstanding preadolescent Christina Ricci as doomy daughter Wednesday. A drolly dark comedy that moves with the fearsome speed of a 1930s screwball, thanks to the surgical precision of Dede Allen’s editing. Part of Screen Time at Metrograph

https://metrograph.com/film/9999003788-s.description: Marker's voyage through memory, history, and video games is a free-flow of images shot largely in Japan (a cat temple, sacred phalluses, horror movies, sleeping subway riders, an animatronic JFK), with detours to Guinea-Bissau, Iceland, and, for an extended homage to Vertigo, San Francisco. An alien travelog? The world’s most profound home movie? There’s nothing quite like it in the history of cinema. “Some of Sans Soleil’s trains carry dozing commuters, others travel to distant planets. The film itself moves like a ride through an ever-shifting landscape, shuttling between dreams and waking, here and there.” —Series curator Genevieve Yue Part of Trains: Local Routes

https://metrograph.com/film/9999003912-t.description: Divorced, depressed, and brutally overworked, hedge fund manager Seok-woo (Gong Yoo) has hardly any time to devote to his young daughter, Su-an (Kim Su-an), so the birthday trip they’re taking together—a 280-mile train ride from Seoul to Busan, where they’re going to meet with her mother—is a very, very big deal. Life or death, in fact, because while en route a zombie apocalypse breaks out across Korea and on the speeding train itself, leaving Seok-woo, Su-an, and a dwindling handful of uninfected passengers to fight for their lives all the way to their final destination… if it’s still there. Jang’s score, mixing electronic and orchestral elements, moving freely from mournful to menacing, and contributing immeasurably to the film’s mounting momentum, is among his very finest. Part of Composed by Jang Young Gyu

https://metrograph.com/film/9999003939-t.description: Inspired by the Dostoyevsky novella of the same title, Ayoade’s noir-inflected sophomore feature gives a dead game Jesse Eisenberg not one but two juicy parts as both a mousy, long-overlooked office drone, Simon James, and his new colleague, the cocksure and charismatic James Simon, who no one other than Simon seems to notice is in fact Simon’s doppelgänger, and who briskly sets about invading every aspect of Simon’s life. The bleakly comic story of a man struggling to get the upper hand over himself, with Eisenberg, in his virtuoso double role, getting more than capable backup from a supporting cast that includes Mia Wasikowska, Wallace Shawn, and Cathy Moriarty. Part of The Office of Emptiness

https://metrograph.com/film/9999003943-d.description: Young lovers Wan and Huen, fresh out of junior high school in the remote, mountainous mining town where they were raised, look forward to a bright future together in their new home of Taipei—only to face first the grim reality of urban life there, then a three-year separation, after Wan is drafted into the Republic of China Army, which ultimately proves fatal to their affections. Based on the personal experiences of frequent Hou co-screenwriter Wu Nien-jen, the poignant, plangent Dust in the Wind has emerged as a popular favorite among Hou’s films, his first collaboration with composer Chen Ming-chang and actor Li Tian-lu, which also features some of Mark Lee Ping-bing’s most hypnotically beautiful tracking shots. Part of Jiā: Histories of Home

https://metrograph.com/film/9999003989-t.description: As country bumpkin police sergeant Kwak Do-won investigates a series of murders that appear to be connected to a strange, sense-deranging sickness that’s going around, local villagers fix the blame on a Japanese drifter suspected of being an evil spirit in Na’s atmospheric tale of demons, shamans, exorcisms, and animated corpses, steeped in ancient east Asian folklore and Christian symbolism. A sporadically hilarious, brilliantly plotted work of insinuating, creeping terror that turns shopworn horror tropes inside out to create something entirely unpredictable and genuinely disturbing. “Korean cinema has a new genre maestro… A supremely unsettling evocation.” —The Guardian Introduction by composer Jang Young Gyu on Saturday, October 3rd Part of Composed by Jang Young Gyu

https://metrograph.com/film/9999003990-t.description: Ozu’s satirical—and ultimately quite touching—portrait of a marriage first seen in a state of quiet unraveling stars Kogure Michiyo and Saburi Shin as a well-off, childless middle-aged couple who find discreet outlets to express their disappointments and resentments towards one another: the Westernized wife through habitual practice of harmless deceptions and put-downs of the husband that she likens to a sluggish carp in a koi pond; her husband by supporting a niece (Keiko Tsushima) in her flight from proposed marriage arrangement interviews. “There’s stillness, and then there’s Ozu stillness. After an argument with her husband, Taeko sets off on a train journey. The stops sweep by, but she doesn’t take notice. Defiantly, petulantly, and a bit woefully, she sits.” —Series curator Genevieve Yue Part of Trains: Local Routes

https://metrograph.com/film/9999004160-c.description: Taking its title from the Spanish proverb “Raise ravens and they will pick your eyes out,” Saura’s lauded allegorical masterwork, set during the twilight of Spain’s Franco dictatorship, stars Ana Torrent (also seen in Spirit of the Beehive, in the same series) as a traumatized eight-year-old, second of three sisters living with a domineering aunt in Madrid following the death of their parents, who feels herself to be drifting freely between the worlds of the living and the dead and is increasingly convinced she has the ability to snuff out her adult persecutors’ lives. “Both an uncanny drama of family dysfunction and a historical parable of the end of Franco-ism… [Geraldine] Chaplin and Torrent are both outstanding.” —The Guardian Part of The Remembered Lives of G. Chaplin & C. Saura

https://metrograph.com/film/9999004195-t.description: The inconvenient corpse, imbued with a sense of tragedy and terror in Hitchcock’s Rope, is the source of borderline-surrealist farce in The Trouble with Harry, his adaptation of Jack Trevor Story’s novel of the same name, a darkly comic tale in which the residents of a small New England hamlet—exteriors were shot on location in Vermont, with the fall foliage radiant in Technicolor—try and repeatedly fail to dispose of a dead body that has appeared in their midst. A rare foray into comedy (albeit of the black variety) for Hitchcock, with Shirley MacLaine, Mildred Natwick, and Jerry “The Beaver” Mathers perfectly embodying a bevy of smalltown American “types.” Part of The Leaves Are Falling

https://metrograph.com/film/9999004396-2.description: A sort-of sequel to Wong’s Days of Being Wild and In the Mood for Love, the ’60s-set 2046 revisits Tony Leung Chiu-wai’s Chow, now a suave science-fiction writer, to chronicle his various affairs with women (including Faye Wong, Zhang Ziyi, and Gong Li), acting as distractions now that his true love, Mrs. Chen (Maggie Cheung, seen in flashback), has disappeared. Intercutting scenes from Chow’s footloose life—several of these taking place on subsequent Christmas Eves—with scenes from his novel-in-progress, set in the titular year, it’s a film of voluptuous melancholy. Part of Like the Wind: Lensed by Christopher Doyle

https://metrograph.com/film/9999004431-o.description: No one wields a ’Scope frame with quite the same flexibility and dynamism as Hark, and the spectacular, Sergio Leone–inspired Once Upon a Time in China—perhaps the crucial film of the 1990s wuxia revival—shows Hark at his most flamboyant, keeping up with the human whirlwind that is Jet Li, here in the role of physician, martial artist, and 19th-century Cantonese folk hero Wong Fei-hung, who’s pitted against unscrupulous gangsters, human traffickers from the West, and his inconvenient feelings for “13th Aunt” Rosamund Kwan. Showstopping set pieces come fast and furious en route to a shoot-the-works shipboard finale; a monumental work of kinetic cinema. Part of Don't Play with Fire: The Films of Tsui Hark

https://metrograph.com/film/9999004546-e.description: Dovzhenko’s final silent feature, which depicts a clash between reactionary landowning peasants and modernizing paupers bringing the first tractor to their corner of the Ukrainian countryside, has by now spawned nearly a century of debate: is it a propagandist paean to the collectivization project in Stalin’s first Five-Year Plan, which would have catastrophic results in the Ukrainian Famine of 1932-33, or, as certain Soviet censors suspected, an on-the-sly celebration of a Ukrainian folk culture grounded in an ancient connection between the peasants and the soil they’ve so long tilled, threatened with impending erasure? What is not up for question is that Earth is among the greatest of films from the silent film canon, its distinct synthesis of Eisenstein, Pudovkin, and Vertov making it something like a summation of what had come before it, while its lyric ode to the natural world and those that live with it in harmony blazes a trail for the Ukrainian Poetic Cinema of the future to follow. 35mm print courtesy of the Filmoteka Narodowa, Warsaw Live musical accompaniment by Fima Chupakhin, piano & synths, and Julian Kytasty, bandura & vocals on Saturday, October 10th Part of Oleksandr Dovzhenko: Earth and Empire

https://metrograph.com/film/9999004567-d.description: Sylvia Chang has one of the finest roles in her formidable career in Huang’s Golden Horse Award–winning intergenerational drama, co-produced by Chang and Hou Hsiao-hsien. Chang’s Jin Aixia is the middle-aged mother of two adult daughters—one, Fan Zuer (Eugenie Liu), raised by her in Taipei, the other, Emma (Karena Lam), given up for adoption and raised in New York—who, after Fan’s tragic death, finds herself the legal guardian of the embryo that her daughter, in the midst of planning for a pregnancy via in vitro fertilization, had left behind. Tender but never maudlin, with a taste (and talent) for structural experiment, Huang’s second feature confirms the writer-director as one of the most impressive up-and-coming talents in Taiwanese cinema. A Dekanalog release Part of Jiā: Histories of Home

https://metrograph.com/film/9999004610-s.description: Fired from his factory job, Ryu (Shin Ha-kyun), a gentle deaf-mute man desperately trying to scrape together funds for his sister’s kidney transplant, falls in with a plan, hatched by his anarchist activist girlfriend (Bae Doona), to kidnap the daughter of the wealthy industrialist who fired him and ransom her for the necessary cash—and in so doing sets off on a path that terminates in an explosion of shockingly visceral violence. A brutal, claustrophobic film of escalating desperation, illustrating with grim logic how an ordinary man can be pushed into acts of extraordinary retaliation, with Bae’s performance bringing some welcome levity to the affair, even as her character acts as the catalyst for catastrophe to come. Introduction by LEENALCHI and a post-screening Q&A with composer Jang Young Gyu moderated by Goran Topalovic, October 3rd Part of Composed by Jang Young Gyu

https://metrograph.com/film/9999004965-f.description: Perhaps the best-loved of Iosseliani’s French productions and the one that earned him the enormously prestigious Prix Louis Delluc, deliciously deadpan formalist comedy Farewell, Home Sweet Home is another of the director’s ensemble narratives, its seemingly disparate, blackout sketch-style segments slowly revealed to be puzzle pieces that form a panorama of high- and lowlife in contemporary Paris. Among the curious characters who flit by is a dissolute upper-class house husband, played by Iosseliani, content to hole up with a bottle and his electric trains while his wife entertains company—a telling image, as the filmmaker here is something like the engineer of a magnificent model train set, transferring from one narrative line to another in some of the most exquisite tracking shots you will ever see. Part of Otar Iosseliani: Fables of Modern Life

https://metrograph.com/film/9999004966-w.description: Based loosely on writer/director Robinson’s memories of being a penniless actor in late ’60s London, Withnail and I stars Richard E. Grant and Paul McGann as two unemployed thesps and Camden Town flatmates—hard-drinking, dissolute Withnail and an unnamed “I,” respectively—who “go on holiday by mistake” at the Lake District home of Withnail’s pompous Uncle Monty (Richard Griffiths), and there commence a program of boozing, bickering, and baiting. Endlessly quotable (“We want the finest wines available to humanity. And we want them here, and we want them now!”), winningly splenetic and shambolic and, taken altogether, about as enjoyable a film of pills, thrills, and bellyaches as you’ll ever find. Part of Going Up the Country

https://metrograph.com/film/9999004975-d.description: Teen runaway Simone (Désirée Nosbusch, entrancingly opaque) loves the Neue Deutsche Welle pop singer known only as “R” (Bodo Staiger)… loves him so much, in fact, that she could just about eat him alive. And when she finally meets her idol—only to be callously treated by him as a disposable sex object—well, Simone gets the chance to really become one with her beloved forever. A hard, cool-to-the-touch, and utterly riveting slow-burn psychological thriller that, newly restored for its first ever US theatrical release, speaks to our age of parasocial obsession, featuring a sinister synth-pop soundtrack by Staiger’s own band, Rheingold, and a last act that’s finger-lickin’ good. Der Fan has been restored in 4K from its original 35mm camera negative by Fun City Editions. The film is presented with its original stereo soundtrack for the first time since its initial German theatrical release in 1982. Introduction by filmmaker Jacqueline Castel on Friday, August 28th Part of That Most Taboo of Red Meats

https://metrograph.com/film/9999004982-p.description: Set in the newly established, vulnerable Republican China of 1913, Peking Opera Blues is a fizzily exuberant, chaotically colorful espionage thriller/screwball romance/slapstick social satire/costume drama pageant that bends genres and genders at will, wending together the stories of three irrepressible female protagonists—played by Sally Yeh, Brigitte Lin, and Cherie Chung, respectively here as a would-be star of the all-male Peking Opera stage, a warlord’s headstrong daughter, and a courtesan who’s copped a case of stolen jewels. Frenetic, filled with whiplash-inducing tonal shifts, frightfully enjoyable and, in the opinion of Quentin Tarantino, “one of the greatest films ever made.” Part of Don't Play with Fire: The Films of Tsui Hark

https://metrograph.com/film/9999004987-t.description: A foundational text of the Taiwanese New Wave, omnibus triptych The Sandwich Man represented a clean break from the cloying sentimentality of most of the country’s studio product, with director’s Hou, Wan, and Tseng each adapting stories from a collection by Huang Chung-ming and addressing, with bracing directness, the harsh realities of contemporary urban life. Hou bats leadoff with the devastating namesake segment, about a man eking out a living as a human advertising board; Tseng’s Vickie’s Hat offers a cautionary tale about the perils of modern convenience, namely imported Japanese pressure cookers; Wan’s The Taste of Apples acquaints us with a family in the Taipei City slums whose only hope for a glimpse of the good life is a bed in the American Navy hospital. Part of Jiā: Histories of Home

https://metrograph.com/film/9999004990-b.description: Winner of the Palme d’Or at Cannes and the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film, Camus’s international arthouse smash transposes the legend of Orpheus and Eurydice to the favelas of Rio de Janeiro and sets the proceedings shimmying along to a bossa nova beat courtesy composers Antônio Carlos Jobim and Luiz Bonfá. Intoxicating in its zestful, go-for-the-gusto vitality, with Breno Mello charming in the title role and Marpessa Dawn every bit as appealing as the ill-fated beloved he’s determined to follow into the underworld. “An almost irrationally infectious retelling of the Orpheus-Eurydice chestnut set during carnival and feverish with hip-swiveling hustle, exploding local color, and sleeve-worn heart.” —The Village Voice Part of Classical Cinema

https://metrograph.com/film/9999004997-s.description: Tsai’s devastating minimalist portrait of urban desolation, destitution and defeat is a gorgeous cinematic lament starring Lee Kang-sheng as a single father of two who ekes out a subsistence living by working as a human signboard while his hungry children wile their days away in the supermarket, where they’ll encounter a protector in the person of manager Chen Shiang-chyi. Part of Jiā: Histories of Home

https://metrograph.com/film/9999004998-n.description: Pasolini’s thrillingly freeform, intellectually adventurous documentary, narrated in the style of thoughts dashed off in a notebook, charts his preparations to make a film of Aeschylus’s Oresteia trilogy in Tanzania, Ethiopia, and Uganda. Forming a trilogy of sorts with previous Greek tragedy adaptations Oedipus Rex and Medea—a trilogy that, in the phrasing of scholar Daniel Humphrey, encapsulates Pasolini’s paradoxical “archaic modernism”—Notes Toward an African Orestes proposes metaphorical parallels between the source texts and events following the emergence of many African nations into independence, and also finds the filmmaker testing his own presumptions and prejudices against the lived experience of African students at the University of Rome. Part of Classical Cinema

https://metrograph.com/film/9999005000-s.description: Nearing-retirement veteran Detective Morgan Freeman and new transfer Brad Pitt track a serial killer with an advanced sense of stagecraft through a sickly, perpetually sodden city of peeling lead paint and lost souls in Fincher’s tour de force, easily one of the most stylistically influential films of the 1990s. “The look of Se7en … came out of this tight working ‘cell’ we created between David, myself, the production designer Arthur Max, and the costume designer Michael Kaplan. The four of us would meet together to discuss the art direction and visual scope of the movie, and we did several sessions like that to establish a unified plan… There was something [about Robert Frank’s photos in The Americans] that interested me, which was related to the grittiness of them, the blandness, the loneliness of a past era and the texture of death.” —Darius Khondji Part of Radical Chiaroscuro: The Work of Darius Khondji

https://metrograph.com/film/9999005003-t.description: Hired by a wealthy collector to authenticate a rarer-than-rare copy of Aristide Torchia’s 17th-century tome The Nine Gates of the Kingdom of Shadows, purported to allow its owner to summon the Devil, New York–based antiquarian book dealer Dean Corso (Johnny Depp) sets off for Europe—and soon finds himself contending with cutthroat cults, suspicious suicides, and a most beguiling Emmanuelle Seigner. “[Polanski] represents the essence of cinematic genius for me… [On The Ninth Gate] I learned how to appreciate the distance between the camera and the actor, and also how to move the camera—or not—at a certain point in the story. I also learned to have a strong sense of the set and its design—that the set can be an actor itself, that it can be filmed like another character in the movie. And I learned the incredible accuracy you can have when cutting from one shot to another.” —Darius Khondji Part of Radical Chiaroscuro: The Work of Darius Khondji

https://metrograph.com/film/9999005004-a.description: Taking over the reins from John Woo, Saigon-born series producer Tsui had a homecoming of sorts with this anxiety-riddled, squib-drenched 1974-set prequel, which shows us A Better Tomorrow protagonist Mark, in his younger and more vulnerable years, running guns into war- and warlord-torn Vietnam. Chow Yun-fat slides back into Mark’s iconic duster like a second skin, Tony Leung Ka-fai enters the franchise as Mark’s cousin, brother-in-arms, and romantic foil, and Anita Mui is in fine fettle as the hardened black marketeer who melts both of their hearts. A lividly angry and downright apocalyptic ending to the trilogy, practically reeking of spent shells and fresh-spilled blood. Part of Don't Play with Fire: The Films of Tsui Hark

https://metrograph.com/film/9999005005-i.description: The final film of Cacoyannis’s “Greek Tragedy” trilogy, following 1962’s Electra and 1971’s The Trojan Woman, adapts Euripides’s Iphigenia in Aulis, with an exceptional Tatiana Papamoschou as the waifish, doe-eyed daughter of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, and Kostas Kazakos and Irene Papas—the latter a throughline in the trilogy—as her royal parents, commanded to sacrifice their daughter so the Greek fleets might set sail for Helen and for Troy. Bringing a naturalistic touch to the lyric drama and grounding it in real locations, including the ruins of Mycenae and the breathtaking Peloponnese coast, Cacoyannis gives us an Iphigenia that’s faithful but not slavishly so, true to the world of antiquity yet bracingly immediate. Print courtesy of the Wisconsin Center for Film and Theater Research Part of Classical Cinema

https://metrograph.com/film/9999005006-t.description: In 1984, American-born, Paris-based artist Elizabeth Lennard traveled to Japan to make a film for French television about Ryuichi Sakamoto, pop star, solo artist, film actor, and film score composer. The result, shot over the course of a frenetic week, was Tokyo Melody, a mosaic work whose structure appears to have been determined by the multi-faceted nature of its subject’s creative practice: at various points we see Sakamoto snapping photographs, cruising through Tokyo on foot or via limousine, performing onstage with Yellow Magic Orchestra, pottering around his house, and in the studio for the recording of his Illustrated Musical Encyclopedia. Made not so long after his collaboration with Nagisa Ōshima on Merry Christmas, Mr. Lawrence, Lennard’s scintillating film, now in a new 4K restoration, captures a pivotal juncture in an extraordinary life. Introduction by composer Paul Grimstad on Saturday, September 26th Part of Sakamoto on Screen Portraits of an Artist

https://metrograph.com/film/9999005007-r.description: An extension of Omori’s short Ryuichi Sakamoto: Last Days, made in close collaboration with Sakamoto’s family, Diaries is an intimate portrait of the subject over the three and a half years following his diagnosis with terminal cancer, shown in archival footage and original material at his New York home, receiving regular chemotherapy treatments in hospital, and continuing through all trials and tribulations his creative work, with longtime friend Min Tanaka heard reading passages from Sakamoto’s journal. A film about living with a finite number of hours ahead that, remarkably, is something other than a doleful threnody; its credits roll to a 1981 song that Sakamoto wrote and performed with Yellow Magic Orchestra: “Happy End.” US premiere Part of Sakamoto on Screen Portraits of an Artist

https://metrograph.com/film/9999005009-p.description: Tensions brew and language becomes a barrier when widowed tai chi master Mr. Chu (Lung Sihung) swaps Beijing for a new life in New York City, where he joins the household of his Americanized son and white daughter-in-law. Lee’s directorial debut evidences the keen eye for generational and cultural differences, as dramatized with compassion and gentle humor, that would distinguish his next two features, The Wedding Banquet (1993) and Eat Drink Man Woman (1994). Part of Jiā: Histories of Home

https://metrograph.com/film/9999005010-j.description: Painter and repeat Sembène collaborator Younousse Sèye plays the title role in this endearing and often very funny study of a woman holding her own in patriarchal Senegalese society. A single mother and successful small business owner, Faat Kiné has every reason to be content with her lot, but her two recently graduated children are adamant in their insistence she remarry, and so our heroine must contend with a parade of unworthy suitors clamoring to relieve her of her precious independence. “We chose Faat Kiné because the film reflects our generation more than Sembène’s previous work. Faat Kiné shows what Senegal looked like in the early 2000s through its vibrant color and comedic tone. Sembène celebrates modern African women’s economic independence while criticizing patriarchal hypocrisy and religious conservatism. The film sparks interesting discussion, and we believe our audience will have deeper thoughts about Sembène’s intentions in making this film.” —Assane Sy and Ahmad Cissé, Jollof Films Post-screening discussion with Jollof Films on Sunday, September 27th

https://metrograph.com/film/9999005011-r.description: His health failing, some six months before his death Sakamoto sat down before a Yamaha grand piano under the direction of his son, Sora, and gave a final command performance before the camera, a career-spanning 20-song set encompassing his time with Yellow Magic Orchestra (a new arrangement of “Tang Poo”), songs heard here for the first time (“BB,” a tribute to Bernardo Bertolucci), and soundtrack compositions for films (“The Last Emperor” and “The Sheltering Sky,” both for none other than “BB”), video games (“Lack of Love”), and even television commercials (“Aubade 2020”). A singularly elegiac concert film, almost hypnotic in its stripped-down simplicity. Q&A with cinematographer Bill Kirstein and producer Albert Tholen moderated by filmmaker Kogonada on Sunday, September 27th Part of Sakamoto on Screen Portraits of an Artist

https://metrograph.com/film/9999005012-s.description: Adapted from the enormously influential author Yu Lihua’s novel Mother and Son, Sung’s film is an enormously compassionate drama about a young mother (Li Hsiang) seen stepping out on her husband by their child, an incident that, in the wake of his long-ailing father’s death and his mother’s subsequent remarriage, feeds a fire of hatred in the boy’s heart. Depicting, with an admirable withholding of judgment and emotional acuity, new tensions arising in a rapidly modernizing society still bound by very traditional notions of feminine self-sacrifice and filial piety, Story of Mother won plaudits for its fingers-on-the-pulse contemporaneity, voted the year’s best Mandarin-language film by an association of Taiwanese critics. Theatrical licenses courtesy of Taiwan Film and Audiovisual Institute Part of Jiā: Histories of Home

https://metrograph.com/film/9999005014-t.description: Jang and Lee Byung-hoon’s propulsive score sets a fire under Na’s unrelenting man-on-the-run thriller that burns hotter with each passing minute. Debt-strapped down-on-his-luck cabbie Gu-nam (Ha Jung-woo), an ethnic Korean living and working in China, agrees to take a contract killing gig from a local gangster (Kim Yoon-seok) that will take him across the Yellow Sea and into South Korea—and in short order finds himself scrambling to keep ahead of cops, crooks, and a bevy of other characters who’d like nothing more than to see his head on a skewer. “Contains two of the most mindbogglingly choreographed, thrillingly extended pursuit scenes—one on foot and one in cars—that I’ve ever seen.” —Amy Taubin, Film Comment Part of Composed by Jang Young Gyu

https://metrograph.com/film/9999005015-a.description: A mob enforcer (Lee Byung-hun, No Other Choice) with a sterling record of loyal service finds himself fighting for his life after sparing the life of his boss’s straying mistress (Shin Min-a) in Kim’s drum-tight neo-noir thriller, unusually grounded by both emotional stakes and a sense of real physical danger in the action set pieces, choreographed for the widescreen with much panache. Jang’s second collaboration with Kim, after The Foul King, earned him and collaborator (and Peach Present collective bandmate) Dalparan Best Music honors from the Busan Film Critics Association, responding to the composers’ sophisticated melange of samba, flamenco, solo cello, and electronic elements. Part of Composed by Jang Young Gyu

https://metrograph.com/film/9999005016-t.description: Already a well-established presence in South Korean music, with an ability to work with equal facility in a variety of idioms (experimental, rock, folk, et. al.), Jang got his start in film composing the distinctive score for Kim’s eccentric, unpredictable, and entirely endearing underdog sports comedy, a barbed commentary on suffocating white-collar culture starring Song Kang-ho (Parasite) as mild-mannered bank clerk Dae-ho, mercilessly pushed around in the office and generally ground down by life… until he gains a new measure of self-worth by beginning to moonlight as a masked “heel” wrestler, his signature move: finding ingenious new ways to cheat in the ring. Part of Composed by Jang Young Gyu

https://metrograph.com/film/9999005017-o.description: The Coens’ country-fried, Depression era, quasi-musical take on The Odyssey borrows its title—and more than a bit of its anarchic sense of humor—from Preston Sturges’s Sullivan’s Travels, choreography cues from Busby Berkeley, and rips a few dozen pages out of the Great American Songbook for good measure.
